structure.title: 5.2 Long-run effects on educational and economic outcomes
Acknowledgments, Supplementary Data, Data Availability Statement, References

observations.statement: The authors describe two difference-in-differences strategies: a within-student before/after comparison for short-run outcomes and an across-cohort comparison (exposed cohorts versus cohorts enrolled five years earlier) for long-run outcomes, each benchmarked against matched control schools.
Causal interpretation is tied explicitly to a standard parallel trends assumption within match groups; the authors say they assess it with raw trend comparisons and event-study specifications.
observations.quote: Causal interpretation of β relies on a standard parallel trends assumption

observations.statement: The short-run design section names differential attrition from the public school system as the key remaining threat and describes how it will be tested with an unbalanced sample and an in-data indicator as outcome.

For long-run outcomes the paper motivates a two-step reporting: a specification with separate interactions for the too-old cohorts to reveal pre-existing school differences, then a specification with school fixed effects that absorbs them.

Nearest-neighbour matching of control schools is justified as reducing differential trend concerns; schools in the same district are excluded because of evidence of spillovers, and the matching variables and their timing (first grading period of the shooting year) are listed.

Two shooting databases (CHDS and Washington Post) are cross-checked, with download dates reported; exclusions (second shootings at a school, off-hours or off-grounds events, a BB-gun incident) are stated one by one with reasons and the resulting event counts.
The shorter event window for the long-run analysis is justified by the need to observe all outcomes through a given age for both exposed and comparison cohorts.

Linkage of school records to college and earnings records uses an anonymised social security identifier; students with invalid identifiers are excluded from the long-run sample and the authors report checking that identifier validity does not differ by exposure.

The short-run sample is a balanced student panel observed from three years before to two years after the event; grade range implied by this requirement and the split of students between shooting and control schools are stated in the text.
Control-school students who were ever enrolled at a shooting school are dropped, and inclusion is based on enrolment at any point in the semester of the shooting rather than the whole year.

The staff analysis restricts to shootings occurring after the October staffing snapshot and to match groups fully observed over the window, treating the shooting year as pre-period; the resulting number of events is stated in a footnote.

Five annual short-run outcomes are defined precisely (absence rate as a ratio of days, chronic absenteeism as a threshold on that rate, grade repetition, days of disciplinary action, school switching excluding structural transitions).
Days of disciplinary action are winsorized at the top percentile to limit outlier influence.

Long-run outcomes are measured once per person at a fixed age (college enrolment and degree by age 26; employment and earnings averaged over ages 24 to 26), with earnings in constant dollars and a separate conditional-on-positive earnings measure.
Test scores are described as available but not used as outcomes because the state test regime changed several times and comparable grades rarely coincide with the shooting schools' grade levels.

Non-attendance at college or non-employment in Texas is coded as zero rather than missing for individuals with valid identifiers absent from the linked files; the authors flag the implications for out-of-state movers.

Main tables report the coefficient, standard error in parentheses and p-value in brackets, a pre-shooting or control-group outcome mean, observation counts and R-squared; notes list the fixed effects, cluster level and how the mean is computed.

Rather than a controls progression, columns are outcomes and rows are cohort-specific interactions; pooled summary estimates across exposure grades are relegated to an appendix table and quoted in text.
observations.locator: Tables 2 and 3; Appendix Table A6 referenced

observations.statement: For school-level staffing regressions the text and figure notes state that school-year cells are weighted by enrolment measured at a fixed date and that errors are clustered by school.

Short-run errors are clustered by school, with the number of clusters (shooting plus control schools) spelled out in the design section; long-run errors are clustered at school-by-cohort, stated without further justification.
observations.quote: Standard errors are clustered by school

observations.statement: For subgroup analyses with few clusters (school resource splits, shooting-type splits) the authors switch to wild cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and note in figure notes that these intervals are not centred on point estimates.

Long-run estimates are additionally assessed with a permutation test that draws placebo treated schools, re-runs the matching and assigns observed shooting dates, repeated many times; results appear in appendix figures.

A balance table compares shooting schools, matched controls and all state schools, with p-values for differences, separately for high and non-high schools; it is in the appendix and discussed in the design section.

Raw trend plots by treatment status and event-study coefficient plots with confidence intervals are both in the main text; the authors explain that rising pre-period trends reflect ageing and stress that they are parallel.
Attrition is examined by plotting the share of students present in each event year by group and by estimating the event study with an in-data indicator as outcome; both appear in an appendix figure.
Lee bounds are computed for the long-run outcomes using the short-run attrition gap as the assumed differential attrition, reported in appendix tables and described as conservative.
observations.locator: Footnote 35; Appendix Tables A7 and A8

observations.statement: Robustness to linear and non-linear violations of parallel trends is checked with the Rambachan and Roth approach, placed in an appendix and cited in a footnote.

Coefficients on the too-old cohorts serve as a placebo-style check for pre-existing school differences in long-run outcomes; left and right panels of each figure show the specification without and with school fixed effects.
Out-of-state migration is checked with an external survey (ACS) at county level around events, using raw plots and an event-study specification, reported in an appendix.
The balanced-panel restriction is relaxed by overlaying unbalanced-panel event-study estimates on baseline estimates in an appendix figure.

Eight alternative matching strategies (extra match variables, exact region match, more controls, reverse order, earlier timing, staff measures, excluding nearest schools) are listed and shown as coefficient plots with the baseline in each panel.
observations.locator: Section 5.3; Appendix Figures A12 to A14

observations.statement: A build-up exercise starts from a parsimonious matching set and progressively adds matching variables toward the baseline, for both short- and long-run outcomes.
observations.locator: Section 5.3; Appendix Figures A15 to A17

observations.statement: The short-run analysis is re-run on the eight-event long-run subsample to show comparability across the two event samples; shooting-type distributions are also compared across samples in an appendix table.
observations.locator: Footnote 15; Section 5.2; Appendix Figure A6, Tables A2 and A5

observations.statement: Heterogeneity is by split-sample re-estimation across student characteristics, school resource medians and shooting types, shown as coefficient plots with the baseline at the top; schools with too few students in a group and incomplete match groups are dropped.
Subgroup effects are also re-expressed relative to subgroup-specific outcome means in an appendix figure to separate level from proportional differences.
For long-run outcomes heterogeneity is limited to student characteristics because the small number of events precludes school- or shooting-level splits; results are in appendix figures.

A mediation-style benchmarking multiplies control-group OLS associations of earnings with college attendance and absenteeism by the estimated treatment effects; the authors explicitly caution that the associations are not causal.
School staffing employment and retention are analysed as mechanism outcomes motivated by the background section's channel discussion, using school-level versions of the baseline equations.
observations.locator: Section 5.4 'Effects on school staff'; Figures 8 and 9

observations.statement: Spillovers are studied by re-running matching and both designs for the six nearest schools grouped in pairs by distance rank, with detail on how control schools for neighbours are chosen in a footnote.
observations.locator: Section 5.4; footnote 44; Appendix Figures A28 to A30

observations.statement: Effects are stated as proportions of pre-shooting or control-group means and compared in a dedicated 'Magnitude comparison' paragraph with studies of police killings, disruptive peers, a mass shooting abroad, and class and teacher quality.
The earnings effect is translated into equivalent standard-deviation changes in class quality and teacher quality from prior work.

The conclusion converts the earnings effect into present-discounted lifetime earnings per exposed student using CPS age-earnings profiles and a stated discount rate, aggregates nationally, and benchmarks against school resource officer spending and per-pupil expenditure.

The authors acknowledge that out-of-state college enrolment, some private institutions and out-of-state employment are unobserved, and organise four sets of evidence to argue that differential migration is unlikely to matter, noting the bias sign is ambiguous.
Earnings measured in the mid-twenties are described as possibly a lower bound for lifetime effects because of the education-earnings trade-off early in careers.
The absence of parent information and of state-wide fear effects (which would affect controls) are flagged as things the design cannot capture.

The authors position the sample as non-mass shootings and compare the shooting-type mix of the long-run subsample with the short-run sample and with all US school shootings to argue representativeness.
observations.locator: Introduction; footnote 7; footnote 15; Appendix Table A2

observations.statement: Tables use no significance stars; p-values are printed in brackets under standard errors, and notes restate the equation estimated, fixed effects, clustering and the basis of the reported mean.

Figures include a map of events, raw trend plots by group, event-study plots with confidence intervals, and subgroup coefficient plots; figure notes report the number of shooting and control schools in each panel and any sample subset.
Staffing figures scale the y-axis to a fixed percentage band of the pre-period mean so that effects are comparable across staff groups.

Appendix material is lettered (Tables A1 onward, Figures A1 onward, Appendices C and D) and holds the event list, school balance table, staff descriptives and most robustness figures; the main text has three tables and nine figures.
The introduction previews every block of results with magnitudes, has a three-strand contribution discussion, and ends with a section roadmap.

Order is background mechanisms, data, design (matching, short run, long run), results (short run then long run with heterogeneity inside each), a separate sensitivity section, then supplemental mechanism and spillover evidence, then conclusion.

Attrition checks, permutation distributions, alternative matching, long-run heterogeneity, spillover figures and honest-DiD sensitivity all live in the online appendix, with the main text summarising them in a sentence or two each.

A Data Availability Statement says the individual-level data are confidential but obtainable by other researchers through a formal application, and that cleaning and analysis code is on Zenodo with a DOI.

Education, higher education and UI earnings records are linked administrative data accessed through a university research centre, named in a footnote and the acknowledgments with a link; shooting databases are public downloads.
Funding source with award number and a disclaimer that views are not those of the data provider are given; no IRB, consent or preregistration statement appears.
The paper text itself does not name statistical software; the only software-related reference is the Zenodo replication package.

gaps: No explicit justification for the school-by-cohort cluster level in the long-run analysis beyond its statement.
No multiple-testing adjustment discussed despite many outcomes and subgroups.
No statistical software named in the paper text.
No IRB, consent or preregistration statement.
Online appendix (Tables A1 onward, Figures A1 onward, Appendices C and D) is not included in the text file, so appendix practices are recorded only from main-text cross-references.

reading.note: All 39 pages of the published article were read, including footnotes, Data Availability Statement and references. The online appendix is not part of the file and could not be read.
